archetype.name: Bubble Team (goalie-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose goaltending and penalty kill keep it near .500 while a low-volume offense and a dead power play cap how high it can climb, which leaves it fighting for the last Metropolitan spots.

report.headline: Sorokin and the PK hold the line; an offense without shots can't push it forward
report.take:
The Islanders are the same team they have been for years, with a better young defenseman. At 7-6-3 they sit fifth in the Metropolitan and 18th on the site. Their Goal Diff / GP of -0.12 matches the record almost exactly, and a Pts vs Goal Diff of -0.1 says the standings aren't lying in either direction. The shape underneath is familiar. The offense ranks 24th by goals a game and the defense 12th. History shows offense ranks of 22, 22, 22, 28 and 26 over the last five seasons, so the scoring problem is a fixture and not a slump.

The goaltending carries the season. Goalies GSAx sits at 8.2, fourth in the league, and the all-situations save % of .905 runs well above the league's .891. Both goalies are contributing: Ilya Sorokin is at 5.2 GSAx over 11 starts and Semyon Varlamov at 4.8 over 5. The penalty kill, fifth at 85.7%, is the other pillar. Both are needed, because the skaters give up more than they create: 28.2 shots against a game (23rd) against 25.4 for (28th). At 5-on-5 the puck is split evenly, with CF % at exactly 50% and xGF % at 49.5%. The Islanders lose the shot battle overall, and the goalies erase most of it.

The numbers hide where the offense breaks down. Shooting % of 11.3% is right at the league's 11.6%, so this isn't bad finishing luck that will turn. The problem is volume, and the power play is the worst of it: 14.6% ranks 29th, and the history shows 12.6%, 16.5% and 15.8% in recent years. Matthew Schaefer (9th of 252 defensemen, 16 points in 26.8 minutes a night) and Bo Horvat (16 points, 49 shots) are the two players driving play. After them the forward group grades D+ and the blueline D, dragged by Adam Pelech (226th, 40.4% xGF) and Ryan Pulock (214th).

The recent trend is a warning. The points have held, at 4-3-3 over the last ten, but the last five allowed 4.0 goals a game, almost a goal worse than the season rate. November opened with five-goal losses to Carolina and New Jersey. Some of that is opponent quality: Edmonton, Dallas, Carolina and New Jersey all came in that span. It also shows what happens when a team that concedes shots doesn't get elite goaltending on a given night. The 87-point pace looks about right, which puts the Islanders in a bubble race where the goalies decide most nights.

strengths.title: Goaltending well above league standard
strengths.body: Goalies GSAx of 8.2 ranks fourth and the team save % sits well above the league average, with both Sorokin and Varlamov in positive territory. This is the franchise's identity rather than a hot streak: 2022-23 and 2025-26 both featured GSAx above 40. Some regression in the 101.2 PDO is possible, but a goalie-driven save edge here has a long track record.

strengths.title: An elite penalty kill
strengths.body: At 85.7% the PK ranks fifth, well clear of the league's 77%. Goaltending feeds it, but the kill also posted 84.2% and 80.8% in past seasons, so the structure travels year to year. Expect it to drift down slightly while staying a clear plus.

strengths.title: Schaefer as the engine
strengths.body: Matthew Schaefer ranks 9th of 252 defensemen, leads the skaters in ice time at 26.8 minutes and has 16 points with 57 shots. No other Islander generates as much offense. He and Horvat are the only two skaters producing like top-line players, and the team's ceiling rests on both of them.

concerns.title: No shots, no power play
concerns.body: The Islanders put 25.4 shots on goal a game, 28th, and the power play converts 14.6%, 29th. Their shooting % is league-average, so this is a chance-creation problem, not bad luck. Five straight seasons of bottom-third offense say a fix won't arrive on its own.

concerns.title: Blueline thin behind Schaefer
concerns.body: The defense group grades D despite Schaefer. Adam Pelech plays over 20 minutes a night at a 40.4% xGF and ranks 226th at his position, and Ryan Pulock sits 214th. Those minutes help explain why the team allows more shots than average and leans so hard on its goalies.

concerns.title: Goals against creeping up
concerns.body: The last five games allowed 4.0 goals a game, and November so far is at 5.0. The opponents were strong, but a team that concedes shots is exposed whenever the save % dips. If this keeps up against weaker teams, the margin-neutral record turns into a losing one.

trend.note: The points rate has barely moved, with the last ten at a .550 points % and the last five at .500. The goal margin has eroded over the recent run, against a tough slate including Edmonton, Carolina and New Jersey.

weekAhead.headline: A California swing against three beatable but different teams
weekAhead.body:
Three road games at San Jose, Los Angeles and Anaheim make the softest-looking week on the board. The Sharks (28th on the site) and Kings (29th) both rank in the bottom ten by goal differential, and the Islanders already split two home games with LA and Anaheim in October, losing the LA game in overtime and beating Anaheim 3-2. Even on the road, the Islanders' goalie advantage should matter in a week like this.

Each stop poses a different problem. San Jose is bad everywhere except in net, where its 7.3 GSAx ranks fifth, and that is exactly the matchup a low-shot offense hates. Los Angeles has the league's worst PK, which is the best chance all season for the 29th-ranked power play to find something. Anaheim is the most dangerous on paper at 10-7-1, but its record rests on a 15.4% shooting rate and a top-ranked power play, with a 44.2% xGF and a .869 save % underneath. The Islanders' PK and goaltending are built to blunt that.

keyMatchups.title: Islanders PP vs Kings' last-place PK
keyMatchups.body: Los Angeles kills 62.5% of penalties, last in the league. The Kings' goaltending grades D- with a GSAx of -6.5. If the Islanders' power play can't produce here, it is hard to see where it will.

keyMatchups.title: Ducks' power play vs NYI kill
keyMatchups.body: Anaheim's power play converts 38.5%, best in the league, and its shooting % ranks second. Its 5-on-5 play is poor and its goalies are 31st by save %. Stay out of the box and the Islanders should control this game; take penalties and the Ducks' finishing can steal it.

keyMatchups.title: Centers against soft defenses
keyMatchups.body: The Kings let centers score the furthest above expectation in the league, and the Ducks rank 30th against wingers. Horvat, Schenn and the wingers around them should get open ice. A forward group graded D+ needs nights like these to fatten its numbers.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the goals against settle back toward the season rate against weaker opponents, or whether the recent leak is real.

restOfSeason.body:
This profile is built to land in the high 80s: our range is 83 to 92 standings points and 35 to 40 wins, with the 87-point pace near the middle. The goaltending and PK are the sustainable parts, backed by years of history. The 101.2 PDO may give a little back, and with shooting already league-average there is no hidden scoring bump waiting. Expect goals to stay around 2.8 to 3.0 a game unless the power play climbs off the floor. We see it reaching 15% to 19%, still below the league average.

The upside path runs through special teams and Schaefer. A power play that merely becomes mediocre would turn some one-goal and overtime losses into wins, and the Islanders play plenty of those. The downside is a goalie slump: with the blueline graded D and shot volume conceded every night, there is no buffer if Sorokin cools off. That makes them a genuine bubble team in a division where Carolina and New Jersey are pulling away and the remaining spots are open.
swingFactors: Power play rising toward league average

confidence.note: Only 16 games, but the profile matches five seasons of history.
